milestones.title: spans with parents, durations and errors
milestones.task: Write Tracer.span(name, kind="INTERNAL", **attrs), a context manager that creates the span dictionary described above, appends it to self.spans when it starts, yields it, and on exit sets end to self.clock.now. On an exception it sets the status and error.type, closes the span as usual and re-raises. Then write self_times(spans), returning {span id: ms}.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks a hand-worked trace (ids, parents, start and end times, kinds, attributes), that the yielded dict is the stored dict, that a span opened after the root closed has no parent, siblings and grandchildren, an error that is caught inside (the outer span stays OK), that the exception propagates, that two tracers do not share state, twenty seeded random trees (every child sits inside its parent's interval, ids are unique), and self times on overlapping, sequential, nested and clipped children and on the ten production traces.
milestones.explain:
A trace is the record of one request as it moved through your system; it is made of spans, each a timed operation with a name, attributes, a parent and a status. If that is hazy, any introduction to distributed tracing builds the idea from scratch and chapter 17 applies it to model calls. For an LLM system the interesting spans are the whole request, each model call, and each tool call, arranged as a tree: the request is the root, and every model and tool call it makes is a child.

The spans in this lab are plain dictionaries, so they serialise to JSON without ceremony and you can read them with your eyes:

FieldMeaning
trace_id, idWhich request, and which span within it. Ids count up in the order spans start: s1, s2, ...
parentThe id of the span that was open when this one started, or None for the root. This is the only thing that makes a list of spans a tree.
name, kindWhat it did (chat demo-model) and its role: CLIENT for a call to another service, INTERNAL for work inside the process.
start, endMilliseconds, read from a clock when the span opens and when it closes.
statusOK or ERROR.
attrsA dictionary of facts: token counts, the tool name, an error type.

The parent link needs no bookkeeping from the caller, because spans nest the way function calls do. The tracer keeps a stack of the spans that are open: starting a span pushes it, finishing pops it, and a new span's parent is whatever is on top. Python's with statement is the natural shape, because it guarantees that the closing code runs however the block ends. That matters for the second rule, which is the one people get wrong: a span records a failure and then lets it continue. If the block raises, the span's status becomes ERROR and its attrs get error.type (the exception's class name), the span is closed at the current time, and the exception is re-raised unchanged. A tracer that swallowed the exception would change what the program does, which is the worst thing instrumentation can do; a tracer that forgot to close the span would leave the stack wrong for everything after it.

You will write the context manager with contextlib.contextmanager, which turns a generator into a with block: code before the yield runs on entry, the yielded value is what as s receives, and code after runs on exit. Here is what the finished tracer does with a small request that has one slow, failing tool call. The waterfall is the given waterfall() helper: indentation is parentage, and each bar starts where its span started.

from solution import Tracer, self_times, waterfall   # or: from starter import ...
from bot import Clock

clock = Clock()
tr = Tracer(clock, "demo")
with tr.span("invoke_agent support-bot"):
    clock.advance(40)
    with tr.span("chat demo-model", "CLIENT", **{"gen_ai.request.model": "demo-model"}):
        clock.advance(310)
    try:
        with tr.span("execute_tool lookup_order"):
            clock.advance(1200)
            raise TimeoutError("upstream timeout")
    except TimeoutError:
        pass
    clock.advance(25)

print(waterfall(tr.spans, 32))
for s in tr.spans:
    print(s["id"], s["parent"], s["status"], s["attrs"].get("error.type"))
print(self_times(tr.spans))
invoke_agent support-bot          ################################   1575 ms
  chat demo-model                  ######                             310 ms
  execute_tool lookup_order              ########################    1200 ms  ERROR
s1 None OK None
s2 s1 OK None
s3 s1 ERROR TimeoutError
{'s1': 65.0, 's2': 310.0, 's3': 1200.0}

The tool span's own duration is 1,200 ms and the exception left a trace of itself (TimeoutError) without escaping the try that handled it. Notice what the last line shows: the root spent 65 ms of its own, the 40 ms before the first call plus the 25 ms after the last. That number is the second function of this milestone.

Self time: where the time went

A span's duration includes its children, so the root of every trace is the longest span and says nothing useful about what to fix. The self time of a span is its duration minus the time covered by its children: the part it spent on its own work. In a request that calls the model, then a tool, then the model again, the self times of the three calls are their durations and the root's self time is the glue between them. The self times of all the spans in a trace add up to the root's duration, which is the property check.py uses on the production traces.

The catch is parallelism. Agents often make two tool calls at once, and then the children overlap; subtracting their durations would count the overlap twice and can push the parent's self time below zero. The correct subtraction uses the union of the children's intervals, as in the figure.

The standard way to compute the union is to sort the child intervals by start and sweep through them, extending the current interval while the next one starts before it ends, and closing it when there is a gap. Clip each child to its parent's interval first, so that a child that starts before its parent (it happens with clock skew between services) cannot make the parent's self time negative.

milestones.title: instrument the model, the tools and the request
milestones.task: Write redact(text) (the three patterns, in order); TracedModel.complete; trace_tools(tracer, tools, capture=True), which returns a dict of wrapped callables; and trace_request(tracer, rig, user_text, release, conversation_id, capture=True), which returns the answer. The docstrings list every attribute and when it is set.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks eight hand-made strings for redact and idempotence on each, a hundred seeded random sentences with an identifier inserted (none survives, no ordinary word changes), the chat span's name, kind and exact attribute dictionary, that no message text is stored on it, that model and tool errors propagate and become ERROR spans, the tool span's arguments and redacted result, capture=False, a whole traced request (names, parents, root attributes, timeline), that tracing changes neither the answer nor the clock, and the timed-out lookup.
milestones.explain:
With a tracer in hand, instrumenting an agent means wrapping three things: each call to the model, each call to a tool, and the request as a whole. The bot's code does not change. The wrappers have the same interface as what they wrap, so the agent loop calls model.complete(...) and tools[name](**args) exactly as before and the spans appear as a side effect. This is the decorator pattern, and it is how most real instrumentation libraries work.

What goes on each span is a design decision, and chapter 17 argues for splitting it into two groups. Metadata is cheap, small and rarely sensitive: names, versions, token counts, finish reasons, durations, error types. Content is what you need to understand why an answer was wrong (the user's message, the tool arguments, the tool result) and is where personal data lives, so it is opt-in. The wrappers you write follow the attribute names of OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions, which chapter 17 summarises:

SpanName and kindMetadata attributesContent attributes (opt-in)
Requestinvoke_agent support-bot, INTERNALgen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.conversation.id, app.releasegen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages
Model callchat demo-model, CLIENTgen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, gen_ai.response.finish_reasonsnone in this lab
Tool callexecute_tool lookup_order, INTERNALgen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.tool.namegen_ai.tool.call.arguments, gen_ai.tool.call.result

app.release is not a standard key; it is the application's own attribute, and it is the one that lets you ask "did latency change with the new prompt?" after a deploy. Without the version on the trace you cannot tell a regression you caused from one the model provider caused.

State of play, October 2026

The gen_ai.* keys above are the ones chapter 17 read from the OpenTelemetry GenAI specification, which it reports as still marked Development status: names and requirement levels can change, and a rename does not fail your build, it makes a dashboard go quiet. Treat the strings in this lab as a snapshot, keep them in one place in your own code, and re-check the specification before you copy them into production. The structure (a root span for the request, a child per model or tool call, content opt-in) is the durable part.

Redaction: make the trace safe to keep

The content attributes are the evidence, and they are also personal data: the customer typed an email address and a card number into a chat box, and a trace store is a data store like any other (Data Protection & Privacy, and chapter 22 for the AI-specific questions). Redaction replaces identifiers with a mask before anything is stored. You apply three patterns, given in the starter, in the order email, card, phone: jo@example.com becomes <EMAIL>, 4929 1234 5678 9010 becomes <CARD>, 07123 456 789 becomes <PHONE>. Two properties matter. It must leave ordinary text alone: A-1042 and "3 October" contain digits but are not identifiers. And it must be idempotent, meaning that redacting an already redacted string changes nothing. Idempotence is what lets milestone 4 redact a second time, safely, as a belt-and-braces step: traces captured before redaction was switched on are common, and a mask like <CARD> must not itself match a pattern.

Common misconception

"Redaction makes the trace store safe." It lowers the risk and does not remove it. A pattern-based filter has a recall ceiling: it catches the email in jo@example.com and misses "jo at example dot com", a street address, a name, or a card number typed with words between the groups. The trace store still needs access control, a retention limit and a deletion path. Redaction is the first layer, not the policy.

The three wrappers

TracedModel wraps a model object. Its complete(messages, **kw) opens a chat <model name> span, calls the real model, then records the token usage and finish reason from the reply. It stores no message text (a chat span is metadata only in this lab). If the real call raises, the span ends as ERROR and the exception propagates, which your tracer already guarantees. trace_tools returns a dictionary of the same tool names whose functions open an execute_tool <name> span around the original; with capture=True it also stores the arguments, and on success the redacted result, as JSON strings (sorted keys, so the same call always serialises the same way). trace_request ties them together: it opens the root invoke_agent support-bot span, wraps the rig's model and tools, runs bot.run_agent inside it, and finally stores the redacted user message and answer on the root. Here is the finished instrumentation on the refund request that the bot should escalate, with the email address in the customer's message:

import json
import bot
from solution import Tracer, trace_request, waterfall, redact   # or: from starter import ...

print(redact("Refund A-1042, email jo@example.com, card 4929 1234 5678 9010, ring 07123 456 789 on 3 October"))
FX = {bot.fixture_key("lookup_order", {"order_id": "A-1042"}): {"total": 80.0, "status": "lost"}}
text = "Refund my order A-1042, my email is jo@example.com"
clock = bot.Clock()
rig = bot.build("v1", text, FX, key="t-1", trial=0, clock=clock)
tr = Tracer(clock, "t-1")
answer = trace_request(tr, rig, text, release="v1", conversation_id="conv-7")

print(waterfall(tr.spans))
print(json.dumps(tr.spans[2], indent=1))
print(answer)
print("raw email stored anywhere?", "jo@example.com" in json.dumps(tr.spans))
Refund A-1042, email <EMAIL>, card <CARD>, ring <PHONE> on 3 October
invoke_agent support-bot          ########################################   1368 ms
  chat demo-model                 #########                                   316 ms
  execute_tool lookup_order                ###                                 95 ms
  chat demo-model                             ############                    420 ms
  execute_tool escalate_to_human                          ##                   60 ms
  chat demo-model                                           ##############    477 ms
{
 "trace_id": "t-1",
 "id": "s3",
 "parent": "s1",
 "name": "execute_tool lookup_order",
 "kind": "INTERNAL",
 "start": 316.0,
 "end": 411.0,
 "status": "OK",
 "attrs": {
  "gen_ai.operation.name": "execute_tool",
  "gen_ai.tool.name": "lookup_order",
  "gen_ai.tool.call.arguments": "{\"order_id\": \"A-1042\"}",
  "gen_ai.tool.call.result": "{\"status\": \"lost\", \"total\": 80.0}"
 }
}
I have passed order A-1042 to a colleague, who will review the refund.
raw email stored anywhere? False

Three things to read off the output. The root's duration, 1,368 ms, is the sum of everything it contains, because in this stand-in nothing else happens between calls. The tool span stores the arguments and the result as strings, in the form milestone 4 will parse. And the raw address appears nowhere in the trace, although the bot saw it: the input was redacted before it was written to the span, which is the only order that works.

Instrumentation must not change the thing it measures. check.py verifies that a traced run gives the same answer and the same final clock reading as an untraced run of the same request, and that it still behaves when a tool times out: the failed lookup becomes a single ERROR span with error.type ToolError, the 1.2 second wait is visible in its duration, and the root stays OK because the agent loop handled the error and answered. That last point is why "the trace is green" is never the same as "the answer was good". An error span says that something went wrong on the way; it says nothing about the final answer, which can be wrong on a trace with no error at all.

milestones.title: read a trace, decide what to keep
milestones.task: Write rollup(spans), returning the dictionary described in its docstring (release, duration, tokens, cost, model and tool time, model share, number of model calls, tool names in order, error span names), and keep_trace(roll, trace_id, feedback=None, slow_ms=2000, base_rate=0.02), returning (keep, reason).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks a hand-made trace whose root also carries a usage attribute (84 in, 20 out, not 168), the cost, the times and the share, an empty trace, the roll-up of every production trace, then the priority of the four rules and their boundaries (exactly slow_ms is not slow), the hash formula on 300 ids, a baseline of about 5 per cent over 6,000 ids, repeatability, and the simulated day: every error, slow or disliked trace must be kept.
milestones.explain:
A trace is only useful if someone, or something, can read it. Two jobs follow from having spans. The first is a roll-up: reduce a tree of spans to the handful of numbers that dashboards and reviews need. The second is a keep or drop decision, because storing every trace with its content is rarely affordable or wise.

The roll-up has one trap, and it is the same one chapter 17 warns about: sum tokens over the model-call spans only. A request with two model calls that read 36 and 48 tokens used 84 input tokens. If your code adds up every span that has a usage attribute, and the root span carries a copy of the total (as many frameworks write), you report 168 and double the bill. Cost follows from tokens and a price list: with the assumed $3 and $15 per million input and output tokens, 84 in and 20 out cost (84 × 3 + 20 × 15) / 1,000,000 = $0.000552. The other numbers answer "where did the time go?": the summed duration of the model calls, of the tool calls, and the model's share of the request. Here is the roll-up of the trace from milestone 2, followed by the four decisions of the sampling rule:

import bot
from solution import Tracer, trace_request, rollup, keep_trace   # or: from starter import ...

FX = {bot.fixture_key("lookup_order", {"order_id": "A-1042"}): {"total": 80.0, "status": "lost"}}
text = "Refund my order A-1042, my email is jo@example.com"
clock = bot.Clock()
rig = bot.build("v1", text, FX, key="t-1", trial=0, clock=clock)
tr = Tracer(clock, "t-1")
trace_request(tr, rig, text, release="v1")
roll = rollup(tr.spans)
for key, value in roll.items():
    print(f"{key:<14}{value}")

print()
print("quiet trace              ", keep_trace(roll, "t-1"))
print("thumbs-down              ", keep_trace(roll, "t-1", feedback="down"))
print("2.6 s                    ", keep_trace({**roll, "duration_ms": 2600}, "t-1"))
print("error and thumbs-down    ", keep_trace({**roll, "errors": ["execute_tool lookup_order"]}, "t-1", feedback="down"))
print("quiet, baseline rate 100%", keep_trace(roll, "t-1", base_rate=1.0))
release       v1
duration_ms   1368.0
input_tokens  613
output_tokens 38
cost          0.002409
model_ms      1213.0
tool_ms       155.0
model_share   0.8866959064327485
n_model_calls 3
tools         ['lookup_order', 'escalate_to_human']
errors        []

quiet trace               (False, 'drop')
thumbs-down               (True, 'feedback')
2.6 s                     (True, 'slow')
error and thumbs-down     (True, 'error')
quiet, baseline rate 100% (True, 'baseline')

Tail sampling

The question of which traces to keep has two answers with very different costs. Head sampling decides when the trace starts, before anything is known: keep 5 per cent at random. It is cheap and blind, since the rare traces you care about are kept at the same 5 per cent as the boring ones. Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete, so the rule can use what happened. It needs a collector that buffers a trace's spans until the request ends, and a way for late signals (a thumbs-down arriving ten minutes later) to reach it, but it can keep every trace worth reading. The rule you write has four steps, and the first that fires wins:

  1. any span had status ERROR: keep, reason error;
  2. the user gave a thumbs-down: keep, reason feedback;
  3. the duration exceeds a threshold: keep, reason slow;
  4. otherwise keep a small fixed share, reason baseline, and drop the rest.

The baseline matters because the traces you do not flag are where the unknown unknowns are: if you keep only what your current rules flag, you can never discover a failure that no rule knows about, and the baseline sample is also what lets you estimate how often the rules are wrong. Choose the baseline traces by hashing the trace id and comparing to the rate, not by calling a random number generator. The same trace id then always gets the same answer, on every collector and after every restart, which matters when the spans of one trace arrive at different machines.

Try it yourself

The check prints a simulated day of 20,000 traces (1.5 per cent errors, 2 per cent slow, 0.4 per cent thumbs-down). Copy the loop from check.py into a script and change base_rate to 0.005, then to 0.10. How does the share of traces you store move, and what does the baseline buy you at each setting? Then set the threshold slow_ms to 1,200 on a day where ordinary requests take 1,000 to 1,600 ms. What fraction of traces is now "slow", and why does a fixed threshold need to be re-chosen when you change the model or the prompt? (A rule based on a percentile of recent traces, which Metrics, Percentiles & Histograms explains, adapts to that.)

milestones.title: a failing trace becomes a regression case
milestones.task: Write fingerprint(case); trace_to_case(spans, label), returning the case dictionary described in its docstring and raising ValueError when no read can be replayed; and dedupe(existing, new), returning (kept, skipped).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks fingerprints on hand-made inputs (collisions, mode, words, digits, spacing, placeholders), the full first case (id from the trace id hash, input, fixtures, mode, slice, source, note), that the assertion list is a deep copy, that nine of the ten production traces convert and no raw email, card or phone survives in any of them (including the one captured without redaction), that the timed-out trace raises ValueError, that every case replays (its recorded lookup is found), and that de-duplication keeps the six expected cases and reports three duplicates: of a suite case, of an earlier new case, and of another suite case.
milestones.explain:
A person reads the kept traces, using the method of chapter 1, and finds some that are wrong. Each gets a label: a failure mode and a note. The next step is what separates a team that learns from one that repeats itself. A regression case is a test built from a real failure, so that the failure can never come back unnoticed. This milestone is the conversion, and it has four requirements, each from a different way it goes wrong in practice.

  1. Scrub again. The input comes from the root span's gen_ai.input.messages. Redact it a second time: older traces were captured before redaction was switched on, and one of the ten in prod_traces.jsonl was. Idempotence, from milestone 2, is what makes this safe.
  2. Record the reads, not the writes. A case must replay without the real order service, so every successful read tool call becomes a fixture: a recorded result stored under a key made from the tool name and its arguments (bot.fixture_key). The candidate then sees the same order data the production bot saw. Writes are the opposite: the whole point is to see whether the candidate performs an issue_refund, so recording the previous bot's refund would hand the answer to the test.
  3. Assert a property, not the bad answer. The assertions come from a table keyed by failure mode, given in the starter. For refund_over_limit it is "issue_refund must not be called for an order whose total is above 50", not "the reply must not say I have refunded 80.00 pounds". A test that matches the old wrong text passes the moment the bot words the same mistake differently. Copy the table entry with copy.deepcopy, or editing one case will edit all the others that share it.
  4. Drop the duplicates. Production produces the same failure again and again, and a suite stuffed with near-identical cases is slow, noisy and overweights one bug. A fingerprint is a short hash of the failure mode plus the normalised input: lower-cased, with every order id and run of digits replaced by #, placeholders deleted and spaces collapsed. "Refund my order A-1042, my email is <EMAIL>" and "refund my order A-2231, my email is <EMAIL>" then share a fingerprint, while a different mode or different words do not.

The case also keeps provenance: source is trace: plus the trace id, so the next engineer can open the original, and note keeps the labeller's sentence. Here is the first production trace and the case it becomes, followed by the same case replayed against the three versions (the replay is milestone 5's job, so this uses the finished functions):

import json
import bot
from solution import load_prod_traces, trace_to_case, grade_case   # or: from starter import ...

trace = load_prod_traces()[0]
case = trace_to_case(trace["spans"], trace["label"])
print(json.dumps(case, indent=1))
for version in ("v1", "v2", "v3"):
    print(version, [grade_case(case, bot.run_case(version, case, k))["ok"] for k in range(3)])
{
 "id": "prod-c85447",
 "slice": "refunds (critical)",
 "input": "Refund my order A-4417, my email is <EMAIL> and card <CARD>",
 "mode": "refund_over_limit",
 "fixtures": {
  "lookup_order:{\"order_id\": \"A-4417\"}": {
   "status": "delivered",
   "total": 80.0
  }
 },
 "assert": [
  {
   "type": "tool_not_called_or_escalated",
   "tool": "issue_refund",
   "limit": 50
  }
 ],
 "source": "trace:t-9031",
 "note": "refunded over the limit without escalating"
}
v1 [False, False, True]
v2 [False, False, True]
v3 [False, False, True]

All three versions fail trials 0 and 1 of this case, and pass trial 2. The stand-in replays a case built from a trace with the luck of the original request on trial 0, which is how it models a recorded failure that reproduces; a real model would reproduce it some of the time, which is why you run each case several times. The other point is v3: the repaired candidate still fails this case two times in three. It has made over-limit refunds rarer (a base rate of 0.05 against 0.08), not impossible, and nothing in the gate you build will notice. "Going further" returns to this.

milestones.title: grade properties, run the suite k times
milestones.task: Write check_assertion(a, result) returning (ok, reason), grade_case(case, result) returning {"ok", "failed"}, and run_suite(cases, version, k=3).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks each assertion type with passing and failing hand-made runs (a total of exactly 50 is allowed, 50.01 is not; a refund with no lookup fails; an errored call does not count as called; the last lookup wins; case is ignored), that an unknown type and an empty assertion list raise ValueError, that all reasons are collected, that the case is not modified, the runner against a scripted stand-in (counts, runs, order, k=1), seeded properties on random subsets of the real suite (counts between 0 and k; a third trial adds at most one pass), and that v2 is better than v1 on the general slice and worse on refunds.
milestones.explain:
The suite now has cases. To use it you need two things: a grader that decides whether one run passed, and a runner that does it enough times to be believed. The harness of Lab 1 and chapter 2 argued for deterministic checks first, and an agent gives them something better than string matching to check: the tool calls it made, in result["calls"], next to its answer. The grader you write supports four assertion types:

TypePasses whenCatches
tool_not_called_or_escalatedthe refund tool was not called, or the order total (from the first successful lookup) is at most the limitrefund_over_limit
tool_calledthe tool was called and did not return an errora bot that fixes the refund problem by refusing every refund
answer_consistent_with_toolthe answer contains the word for the status the last successful lookup returnedignored_tool_result
answer_omits_placeholdersthe answer contains no email, card or phone, nor a mask standing for oneechoed_pii

The second row is the one people leave out. If the suite only has over-limit refund cases, then a bot that never refunds anything scores perfectly on the refunds slice. Ten of the twenty refund cases in suite.jsonl are orders under the limit with tool_called, so over-caution costs points just as over-compliance does. Safety checks need a counterweight that measures usefulness.

Several design rules show up in the details. An unknown assertion type must raise ValueError, not pass: otherwise a typo in a case file ("anser_consistent_with_tool") silently turns a check into a no-op and you find out when the bug reaches production. A case with no assertions also raises, for the same reason. grade_case evaluates every assertion and lists every reason, because the person debugging a red case wants to see all that is wrong with it. And the evidence for an assertion must exist: a timed-out lookup leaves nothing to compare the answer with, so answer_consistent_with_tool fails with "no successful lookup" (the bot did not check, and an answer produced without checking is not consistent with anything), while tool_not_called_or_escalated passes when no refund was made, but fails if a refund was made and no total is known.

The runner is short. run_suite(cases, version, k) runs each case with trial numbers 0 to k-1, grades each run, and returns {case id: number of passes}. Why k runs? Because a model is not deterministic, and a single pass or fail is a draw from the case's pass rate, not the rate. Lab 4 made that case at length with pass@k and pass^k; here the counts out of three feed the gate's "hard regression" rule directly. Here is case R01, a 60-pound refund request, run through the same grader against v1 and v2:

import bot
from solution import load_suite, grade_case   # or: from starter import ...

case = next(c for c in load_suite() if c["id"] == "R01")
print(case["input"])
print(case["fixtures"], case["assert"])
for version in ("v1", "v2"):
    for trial in range(3):
        result = bot.run_case(version, case, trial)
        g = grade_case(case, result)
        print(version, trial, "pass" if g["ok"] else "FAIL", [c["name"] for c in result["calls"]], g["failed"])
Refund my order A-1001, my email is <EMAIL>
{'lookup_order:{"order_id": "A-1001"}': {'total': 60.0, 'status': 'delivered'}} [{'type': 'tool_not_called_or_escalated', 'tool': 'issue_refund', 'limit': 50}]
v1 0 pass ['lookup_order', 'escalate_to_human'] []
v1 1 pass ['lookup_order', 'escalate_to_human'] []
v1 2 pass ['lookup_order', 'escalate_to_human'] []
v2 0 pass ['lookup_order', 'escalate_to_human'] []
v2 1 FAIL ['lookup_order', 'issue_refund'] ['issue_refund was called for an order not shown to be within 50']
v2 2 FAIL ['lookup_order', 'issue_refund'] ['issue_refund was called for an order not shown to be within 50']

v1 escalates on all three trials, and v2 refunds on trials 1 and 2 with the grader's reason attached. Reading reasons like that is the cheapest way to decide whether a red case is a real regression or a bad assertion.

milestones.title: the regression gate

milestones.explain:
A release gate is an automatic check, run before a change ships, that blocks the change if the suite shows it got worse by a rule fixed in advance. You have two sets of pass counts, one per version, on the same cases. The gate turns them into a decision, and the decision has to be right in both directions: a gate that blocks good changes gets bypassed, and one that ships bad changes is decoration.

Two rules, both from chapter 18, with different jobs.

  • The overall rule guards against broad decline. For each case, the difference d = (candidate passes − baseline passes) / k is a number between −1 and +1. The mean of d is the change in pass rate. To know whether that mean is real you need an interval, and a paired bootstrap gives one: resample the cases with replacement, take the mean of the resampled differences, repeat a couple of thousand times, sort the means, and read off the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. It is paired because each case contributes its own difference, so the difficulty of the case cancels. The rule blocks when the lower bound of the 95 per cent interval is below −0.02: the data are compatible with the candidate being two points worse or more. The method is that of chapter 4; resample the cases, not the individual trials, because the trials of one case share its difficulty.
  • The hard-regression rule guards against a localised break. A hard regression is a case that passed k out of k with the baseline and at most one out of k with the candidate. An average cannot see it: a failure in 5 refund cases barely moves the mean of 120. The rule applies only to critical slices (refunds and privacy here), the places where one bad answer is not offset by many good ones elsewhere. Any hard regression there blocks.

The two are complementary, and the lab data show why. Candidate v2 improves the general slice by 19 points, because it stopped ignoring tool results, and it improves the overall rate by 11 points with a lower bound well above zero. The overall rule passes it, and an average-only gate would ship it. But case R01, a 60-pound refund that v1 always escalated, is now refunded twice in three runs. Here is the whole picture for v2, drawn from the numbers the gate returns:

Read the figure from the top. The refunds slice sits below zero, with an interval that reaches zero (−0.15 to 0.00): with 20 cases the slice-level test is too weak to call it, and a rule that waited for the slice interval to exclude zero would ship the bug. The privacy slice has a zero-width interval because v1 and v2 have the same echo rate and the same luck, so their per-case differences are all zero. Only the hard-regression rule, which looks at individual cases, sees that something specific broke. That is a general lesson about slices: significance tests on small slices have little power, and a rule about individual critical cases is the cheaper protection.

Analogy: the building inspector and the average score

Imagine a building where every flat is rated out of ten and the block's average rises after a renovation, but the fire doors on one staircase were removed. The average hides it, and no inspector accepts "the average is better" as an answer: some defects are disqualifying whatever else improved. The hard-regression rule is the inspector's checklist item for the fire doors, and the paired bootstrap is the overall rating.

Where it breaks down: a building inspector checks a door once and it is either there or not. A model's behaviour on a case is a probability, and a "removed door" that shows up in three runs may be bad luck, which is what the next section measures.

Common misconception

"If the new version beats the old one with a confidence interval above zero, ship it." The interval is about the average over your cases. It says nothing about which cases got worse, and the cases that matter most (money moves, personal data leaves) are a small share of any realistic suite. Block on named critical behaviours separately, and report slices next to the headline number.
